claim: Serotonin (5-HT) is one of the major neuromodulators present in the mammalian brain.
source: Serotonin (5-HT) is one of the major neuromodulators present in the mammalian brain and has been shown to play a role in multiple physiological processes.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in neuroscience supported by extensive literature.

claim: 5-HT has been shown to play a role in multiple physiological processes.
source: Serotonin (5-HT) is one of the major neuromodulators present in the mammalian brain and has been shown to play a role in multiple physiological processes.
evidence: This is supported by general scientific knowledge about serotonin function.

claim: The mechanisms by which 5-HT modulates cortical network activity are not yet fully understood.
source: The mechanisms by which 5-HT modulates cortical network activity, however, are not yet fully understood.
evidence: This statement acknowledges a gap in current scientific understanding.

claim: Slow oscillations (SOs) are a synchronized cortical network activity universally present across species.
source: We investigated the effects of 5-HT on slow oscillations (SOs), a synchronized cortical network activity universally present across species.
evidence: This is supported by established neuroscience literature on slow oscillations.

claim: SOs are observed during anesthesia.
source: SOs are observed during anesthesia and are considered to be the default cortical activity pattern.
evidence: This is a well-documented phenomenon in neuroscience.

claim: SOs are considered to be the default cortical activity pattern.
source: SOs are observed during anesthesia and are considered to be the default cortical activity pattern.
evidence: This is supported by neuroscience literature on cortical activity patterns.

claim: MDMA and fenfluramine inhibit SOs within the entorhinal cortex (EC) in anesthetized mice.
source: We discovered that (±)3,4-methylenedioxymethamphetamine (MDMA) and fenfluramine, two potent 5-HT releasers, inhibit SOs within the entorhinal cortex (EC) in anesthetized mice.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: MDMA and fenfluramine are two potent 5-HT releasers.
source: We discovered that (±)3,4-methylenedioxymethamphetamine (MDMA) and fenfluramine, two potent 5-HT releasers, inhibit SOs within the entorhinal cortex (EC) in anesthetized mice.
evidence: This is established pharmacological knowledge about these compounds.

claim: Somatostatin-expressing (Sst) interneurons activated by the 5-HT2A receptor (5-HT2AR) play an important role in the suppression of SOs.
source: Combining opto- and pharmacogenetic manipulations with in vitro electrophysiological recordings, we uncovered that somatostatin-expressing (Sst) interneurons activated by the 5-HT2A receptor (5-HT2AR) play an important role in the suppression of SOs.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data from optogenetic and pharmacogenetic experiments.

claim: 5-HT2AR signaling is involved in the etiology of different psychiatric disorders.
source: Since 5-HT2AR signaling is involved in the etiology of different psychiatric disorders and mediates the psychological effects of many psychoactive serotonergic drugs, we propose that the newly discovered link between Sst interneurons and 5-HT will contribute to our understanding of these complex topics.
evidence: This is supported by existing literature on 5-HT2AR and psychiatric disorders.

claim: 5-HT2AR mediates the psychological effects of many psychoactive serotonergic drugs.
source: Since 5-HT2AR signaling is involved in the etiology of different psychiatric disorders and mediates the psychological effects of many psychoactive serotonergic drugs, we propose that the newly discovered link between Sst interneurons and 5-HT will contribute to our understanding of these complex topics.
evidence: This is supported by pharmacological literature on serotonergic drugs.

claim: Projections originating from the Raphe nuclei innervate all cortical and sub-cortical areas.
source: Projections originating from the Raphe nuclei, the brain-stem structure that comprises the majority of 5-HT releasing neurons in the brain, innervate all cortical and sub-cortical areas (Descarries et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Descarries et al., 2010.

claim: The Raphe nuclei comprise the majority of 5-HT releasing neurons in the brain.
source: Projections originating from the Raphe nuclei, the brain-stem structure that comprises the majority of 5-HT releasing neurons in the brain, innervate all cortical and sub-cortical areas (Descarries et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Descarries et al., 2010.

claim: 5-HT levels in the brain are closely linked to the sleep-wake cycle.
source: 5-HT levels in the brain are closely linked to the sleep-wake cycle: the activity of serotonergic raphe neurons is increased during wakefulness, decreased during slow-wave sleep (SWS) and virtually silent during REM sleep (McGinty and Harper, 1976; Oikonomou et al., 2019; Unger et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to McGinty and Harper, 1976; Oikonomou et al., 2019; Unger et al., 2020.

claim: The activity of serotonergic raphe neurons is increased during wakefulness.
source: 5-HT levels in the brain are closely linked to the sleep-wake cycle: the activity of serotonergic raphe neurons is increased during wakefulness, decreased during slow-wave sleep (SWS) and virtually silent during REM sleep (McGinty and Harper, 1976; Oikonomou et al., 2019; Unger et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to McGinty and Harper, 1976; Oikonomou et al., 2019; Unger et al., 2020.

claim: The activity of serotonergic raphe neurons is decreased during slow-wave sleep (SWS).
source: 5-HT levels in the brain are closely linked to the sleep-wake cycle: the activity of serotonergic raphe neurons is increased during wakefulness, decreased during slow-wave sleep (SWS) and virtually silent during REM sleep (McGinty and Harper, 1976; Oikonomou et al., 2019; Unger et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to McGinty and Harper, 1976; Oikonomou et al., 2019; Unger et al., 2020.

claim: The activity of serotonergic raphe neurons is virtually silent during REM sleep.
source: 5-HT levels in the brain are closely linked to the sleep-wake cycle: the activity of serotonergic raphe neurons is increased during wakefulness, decreased during slow-wave sleep (SWS) and virtually silent during REM sleep (McGinty and Harper, 1976; Oikonomou et al., 2019; Unger et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to McGinty and Harper, 1976; Oikonomou et al., 2019; Unger et al., 2020.

claim: SWS is generally associated with 'synchronized' patterns of activity, characterized by low-frequency global fluctuations.
source: Cortical activity is also influenced by the behavioral state of the animal: SWS is generally associated with 'synchronized' patterns of activity, characterized by low-frequency global fluctuations, whereas active wakefulness and REM sleep feature 'desynchronized' network activity, in which low-frequency fluctuations are absent.
evidence: This is established knowledge in neuroscience about cortical activity patterns.

claim: Active wakefulness and REM sleep feature 'desynchronized' network activity, in which low-frequency fluctuations are absent.
source: Cortical activity is also influenced by the behavioral state of the animal: SWS is generally associated with 'synchronized' patterns of activity, characterized by low-frequency global fluctuations, whereas active wakefulness and REM sleep feature 'desynchronized' network activity, in which low-frequency fluctuations are absent.
evidence: This is established knowledge in neuroscience about cortical activity patterns.

claim: The shifting of cortical networks between different patterns of activity is controlled, at least in part, by neuromodulators.
source: The shifting of cortical networks between different patterns of activity is controlled, at least in part, by neuromodulators (Tukker et al., 2020; Lee and Dan, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Tukker et al., 2020; Lee and Dan, 2012.

claim: Acetylcholine (ACh) can profoundly alter cortical network activity by inducing desynchronization via activation of Sst interneurons.
source: For instance, Acetylcholine (ACh) can profoundly alter cortical network activity by inducing desynchronization via activation of Sst interneurons (Chen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Chen et al., 2015.

claim: ACh is not solely responsible for suppressing cortical synchronized activity, as lesions of cholinergic neurons are not sufficient to abolish desynchronization.
source: However, ACh is not solely responsible for suppressing cortical synchronized activity, as lesions of cholinergic neurons are not sufficient to abolish desynchronization (Kaur et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kaur et al., 2008.

claim: Blocking ACh and 5-HT transmission at the same time causes a continuous 'synchronized' cortical state, even during active behavior.
source: On the other hand, blocking ACh and 5-HT transmission at the same time causes a continuous 'synchronized' cortical state, even during active behavior, thus suggesting that 5-HT plays an important role in mediating transitions between different network states (Vanderwolf and Baker, 1986).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Vanderwolf and Baker, 1986.

claim: 5-HT plays an important role in mediating transitions between different network states.
source: On the other hand, blocking ACh and 5-HT transmission at the same time causes a continuous 'synchronized' cortical state, even during active behavior, thus suggesting that 5-HT plays an important role in mediating transitions between different network states (Vanderwolf and Baker, 1986).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental result cited from Vanderwolf and Baker, 1986.

claim: Electrical and optogenetic stimulation of the Raphe nuclei reduce low frequency (1–10 Hz) power in the cortex.
source: In agreement with this line of thought, electrical and optogenetic stimulation of the Raphe nuclei reduce low frequency (1–10 Hz) power in the cortex, implying a reduction in neuronal synchronization at these frequencies (Puig et al., 2010; Grandjean et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Puig et al., 2010; Grandjean et al., 2019.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of serotonergic neurons is sufficient to awaken mice from SWS.
source: Moreover, optogenetic stimulation of serotonergic neurons is sufficient to awaken mice from SWS (Oikonomou et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Oikonomou et al., 2019.

claim: SOs are a network oscillation characterized by synchronized transitions (<1 Hz) between periods of high activity (upstates) and relative quiescence (downstates).
source: Here, we used electrophysiological techniques together with pharmacology, optogenetics, and pharmacogenetics to investigate the effect of 5-HT on slow oscillations (SOs), a network oscillation characterized by synchronized transitions (<1 Hz) between periods of high activity (upstates) and relative quiescence (downstates) (Steriade et al., 1993; Neske, 2015; Isomura et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Steriade et al., 1993; Neske, 2015; Isomura et al., 2006.

claim: SOs are a global phenomenon observed throughout the cerebral cortex.
source: SOs are a global phenomenon observed throughout the cerebral cortex and are considered to be the default emergent activity of cortical networks during SWS and anesthesia (Neske, 2015; Sanchez-Vives et al., 2017; Wolansky et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Neske, 2015; Sanchez-Vives et al., 2017; Wolansky et al., 2006.

claim: SOs are considered to be the default emergent activity of cortical networks during SWS and anesthesia.
source: SOs are a global phenomenon observed throughout the cerebral cortex and are considered to be the default emergent activity of cortical networks during SWS and anesthesia (Neske, 2015; Sanchez-Vives et al., 2017; Wolansky et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Neske, 2015; Sanchez-Vives et al., 2017; Wolansky et al., 2006.

claim: SOs can be recorded in the mEC both under anesthesia and in acutely prepared cortical slices.
source: We performed our experiments in the medial entorhinal cortex (mEC), a region where SOs can be recorded both under anesthesia and in acutely prepared cortical slices (Tahvildari et al., 2012; Beed et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Tahvildari et al., 2012; Beed et al., 2020.

claim: Pyramidal neurons located in L3 of mEC provide the excitatory drive underlying each upstate.
source: Pyramidal neurons located in L3 of mEC provide the excitatory drive underlying each upstate (Namiki et al., 2013; Beed et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Namiki et al., 2013; Beed et al., 2020.

claim: mEC comprises different types of inhibitory GABAergic neurons that can be grouped into three main classes according to immunoreactivity: parvalbumin (PV), somatostatin (Sst), and 5-HT3.
source: Similarly to other mammalian cortical areas, mEC comprises different types of inhibitory GABAergic neurons that can be grouped into three main classes according to immunoreactivity: parvalbumin (PV), somatostatin (Sst), and 5-HT3 (Miao et al., 2017; Rudy et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Miao et al., 2017; Rudy et al., 2011.

claim: Most PV neurons target the soma and the spike initiation zone, have low input resistance and minimal spike frequency adaptation.
source: Most PV neurons target the soma and the spike initiation zone, have low input resistance and minimal spike frequency adaptation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PV neuron properties.

claim: Sst neurons are divided into two groups, one showing features similar to PV interneurons and a second one (i.e. Martinotti cells) that tend to form synapses onto the dendritic trees of their target cells, have high input resistance and show a considerable adaptation.
source: Sst neurons are divided into two groups, one showing features similar to PV interneurons and a second one (i.e. Martinotti cells) that, in contrast, tend to form synapses onto the dendritic trees of their target cells, have high input resistance and show a considerable adaptation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Sst neuron properties.

claim: 5-HT3 neurons are usually located in the superficial layers, have high input resistance and mixed adaptation.
source: 5-HT3 neurons are usually located in the superficial layers, have high input resistance and mixed adaptation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about 5-HT3 neuron properties.

claim: All different classes of interneurons are depolarized during upstates.
source: While these different classes of interneurons are all depolarized during upstates, PV interneurons receive decidedly the strongest excitation (Tahvildari et al., 2012; Neske et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Tahvildari et al., 2012; Neske et al., 2015.

claim: PV interneurons receive decidedly the strongest excitation during upstates.
source: While these different classes of interneurons are all depolarized during upstates, PV interneurons receive decidedly the strongest excitation (Tahvildari et al., 2012; Neske et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Tahvildari et al., 2012; Neske et al., 2015.

claim: Recurrent excitation and temporal summation of inputs contribute to the transition from downstate to upstate.
source: Recurrent excitation and temporal summation of inputs contribute to the transition from downstate to upstate (Sanchez-Vives et al., 2017; Tukker et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sanchez-Vives et al., 2017; Tukker et al., 2020.

claim: L5a neurons do not participate in SOs.
source: This excitation propagates to L5 and differentially entrains L5a and L5b excitatory neurons. L5a neurons do not participate in SOs, whereas L5b neurons are steadily synchronized.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental observations in the study.

claim: L5b neurons are steadily synchronized during SOs.
source: This excitation propagates to L5 and differentially entrains L5a and L5b excitatory neurons. L5a neurons do not participate in SOs, whereas L5b neurons are steadily synchronized.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental observations in the study.

claim: Both intrinsic and synaptic mechanisms have been implicated in upstate termination.
source: Both intrinsic and synaptic mechanisms have been implicated in upstate termination (Neske, 2015; Tukker et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Neske, 2015; Tukker et al., 2020.

claim: Activity-dependent K+ channels decrease excitability of neurons over time causing a generalized reduction of facilitation.
source: Activity-dependent K+ channels decrease excitability of neurons over time causing a generalized reduction of facilitation (Neske, 2015; Harris and Thiele, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Neske, 2015; Harris and Thiele, 2011.

claim: Blockage of GABAB receptors significantly extends upstate duration.
source: At the same time, blockage of GABAB receptors significantly extends upstate duration (Craig et al., 2013) and inhibitory drive has been observed to increase during upstate termination (Lemieux et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Craig et al., 2013.

claim: Inhibitory drive has been observed to increase during upstate termination.
source: At the same time, blockage of GABAB receptors significantly extends upstate duration (Craig et al., 2013) and inhibitory drive has been observed to increase during upstate termination (Lemieux et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lemieux et al., 2015.

claim: Sst interneurons, and in particular Martinotti cells, are characterized by strongly facilitating synapses.
source: Sst interneurons, and in particular Martinotti cells, characterized by strongly facilitating synapses (Beierlein et al., 2003; Gibson et al., 1999) have been proposed as an important source of inhibition in the termination of upstates (Melamed et al., 2008; Krishnamurthy et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Beierlein et al., 2003; Gibson et al., 1999.

claim: Sst interneurons have been proposed as an important source of inhibition in the termination of upstates.
source: Sst interneurons, and in particular Martinotti cells, characterized by strongly facilitating synapses (Beierlein et al., 2003; Gibson et al., 1999) have been proposed as an important source of inhibition in the termination of upstates (Melamed et al., 2008; Krishnamurthy et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Melamed et al., 2008; Krishnamurthy et al., 2012.

claim: MDMA and fenfluramine suppress SOs in anesthetized mice.
source: Our results show that (±)3,4-methylenedioxymethamphetamine (MDMA) and fenfluramine (Fen), two substitute amphetamines that induce robust 5-HT release, suppress SOs in anesthetized mice and, concurrently, activate a small group of neurons characterized by an intermediate waveform shape.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: MDMA and fenfluramine concurrently activate a small group of neurons characterized by an intermediate waveform shape.
source: Our results show that (±)3,4-methylenedioxymethamphetamine (MDMA) and fenfluramine (Fen), two substitute amphetamines that induce robust 5-HT release, suppress SOs in anesthetized mice and, concurrently, activate a small group of neurons characterized by an intermediate waveform shape.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: 5-HT inhibits SOs in the mEC.
source: Using cortical slices in vitro, we demonstrate that 5-HT inhibits SOs in the mEC and that Sst interneurons, activated by 5-HT2AR, are involved in the modulatory effect of 5-HT.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data from in vitro experiments.

claim: Sst interneurons, activated by 5-HT2AR, are involved in the modulatory effect of 5-HT on SOs.
source: Using cortical slices in vitro, we demonstrate that 5-HT inhibits SOs in the mEC and that Sst interneurons, activated by 5-HT2AR, are involved in the modulatory effect of 5-HT.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data from in vitro experiments.

claim: Previous studies have shown that parvalbumin (PV) interneurons are excited by 5-HT2AR.
source: While previous studies have shown that parvalbumin (PV) interneurons are excited by 5-HT2AR (Puig et al., 2010; Athilingam et al., 2017), our results identify cortical Sst interneurons as novel targets of the 5-HT neuromodulatory system via 5-HT2AR.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Puig et al., 2010; Athilingam et al., 2017.

claim: Cortical Sst interneurons are novel targets of the 5-HT neuromodulatory system via 5-HT2AR.
source: While previous studies have shown that parvalbumin (PV) interneurons are excited by 5-HT2AR (Puig et al., 2010; Athilingam et al., 2017), our results identify cortical Sst interneurons as novel targets of the 5-HT neuromodulatory system via 5-HT2AR.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Under urethane anesthesia, EC displays SOs.
source: Under urethane anesthesia, EC, like the rest of the cortex, displays SOs (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Upstates were present synchronously in the local field potential (LFP) of all the recording channels.
source: As expected, we found that upstates were present synchronously in the local field potential (LFP) of all the recording channels (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), and that every upstate coincided with large increases in population spiking activity (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Figure 1B.

claim: Every upstate coincided with large increases in population spiking activity.
source: As expected, we found that upstates were present synchronously in the local field potential (LFP) of all the recording channels (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), and that every upstate coincided with large increases in population spiking activity (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: 5-HT does not cross the blood brain barrier.
source: 5-HT does not cross the blood brain barrier (Hardebo and Owman, 1980), therefore, to understand the effect of 5-HT on SOs we used MDMA, a potent presynaptic 5-HT releaser and popular recreational drug (Green et al., 2003) that has shown promising results in the treatment of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) (Inserra et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hardebo and Owman, 1980.

claim: MDMA is a potent presynaptic 5-HT releaser and popular recreational drug.
source: 5-HT does not cross the blood brain barrier (Hardebo and Owman, 1980), therefore, to understand the effect of 5-HT on SOs we used MDMA, a potent presynaptic 5-HT releaser and popular recreational drug (Green et al., 2003) that has shown promising results in the treatment of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) (Inserra et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Green et al., 2003.

claim: MDMA has shown promising results in the treatment of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD).
source: 5-HT does not cross the blood brain barrier (Hardebo and Owman, 1980), therefore, to understand the effect of 5-HT on SOs we used MDMA, a potent presynaptic 5-HT releaser and popular recreational drug (Green et al., 2003) that has shown promising results in the treatment of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) (Inserra et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Inserra et al., 2021.

claim: Intraperitoneal injections of MDMA (1.25 mg/kg) caused a strong suppression of upstate incidence.
source: Intraperitoneal injections of MDMA (1.25 mg/kg) caused a strong suppression of upstate incidence (Figure 1E–H), a decrease in power of low frequencies (1–20 Hz) (Figure 1F), and a reduction of population spiking activity (Figure 1G–I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E–H.

claim: Intraperitoneal injections of MDMA (1.25 mg/kg) caused a decrease in power of low frequencies (1–20 Hz).
source: Intraperitoneal injections of MDMA (1.25 mg/kg) caused a strong suppression of upstate incidence (Figure 1E–H), a decrease in power of low frequencies (1–20 Hz) (Figure 1F), and a reduction of population spiking activity (Figure 1G–I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Intraperitoneal injections of MDMA (1.25 mg/kg) caused a reduction of population spiking activity.
source: Intraperitoneal injections of MDMA (1.25 mg/kg) caused a strong suppression of upstate incidence (Figure 1E–H), a decrease in power of low frequencies (1–20 Hz) (Figure 1F), and a reduction of population spiking activity (Figure 1G–I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G–I.

claim: MDMA causes the release of dopamine and noradrenaline (NE), although to a much lesser extent than 5-HT.
source: In addition to 5-HT, MDMA has been shown to cause the release of other neuromodulators, such as dopamine and noradrenaline (NE), although to a much lesser extent (Green et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Green et al., 2003.

claim: Fenfluramine is a more selective 5-HT releaser than MDMA.
source: To test whether the effect of MDMA was mediated specifically by 5-HT, we repeated the experiment using Fen (5 mg/kg), a more selective 5-HT releaser (Rothman and Baumann, 2002; Heifets et al., 2019; Baumann et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Rothman and Baumann, 2002; Heifets et al., 2019; Baumann et al., 2000.

claim: Intraperitoneal injection of Fen (5 mg/kg) had a comparably strong suppressive effect on both the occurrence of upstates and population spiking activity.
source: Intraperitoneal injection of Fen had a comparably strong suppressive effect on both the occurrence of upstates and population spiking activity (Figure 1H–I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1H–I.

claim: Both Fen and MDMA significantly decreased LFP power in the delta and theta frequency ranges.
source: Given the similarity of the observed effects, we grouped the results of Fen and MDMA application and found that both of these drugs significantly decreased LFP power in the delta and theta frequency ranges (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The duration and area of upstates were significantly reduced by Fen and MDMA.
source: Furthermore, the duration and area of upstates were also significantly reduced (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Drug injections differentially affected spiking rates of recorded units: while spiking decreased in most units ('non-activated'), a small group of units ('activated') responded in the opposite fashion (n = 31/355, 8.7%).
source: We found that drug injections differentially affected spiking rates (Figure 2A) of recorded units: while spiking decreased in most units ('non-activated'), a small group of units ('activated') responded in the opposite fashion (n = 31/355, 8.7%).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The cumulative distribution of TP latencies of 'activated' units was significantly different from both Exc and Int groups.
source: The cumulative distribution of TP latencies of 'activated' units was significantly different from both Exc and Int groups (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The average TP latency of 'activated' units was situated in between the Int and Exc groups.
source: Specifically, the average TP latency of 'activated' units was situated in between the Int and Exc groups (Figure 2B–D, Figure 2—figure supplement 2), possibly suggesting a non-FS interneuron identity (Trainito et al., 2019; Kvitsiani et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B–D, Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The intermediate TP latency of 'activated' units possibly suggests a non-FS interneuron identity.
source: Specifically, the average TP latency of 'activated' units was situated in between the Int and Exc groups (Figure 2B–D, Figure 2—figure supplement 2), possibly suggesting a non-FS interneuron identity (Trainito et al., 2019; Kvitsiani et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data and supported by citations to Trainito et al., 2019; Kvitsiani et al., 2013.

claim: Units with intermediate TP latency (between 0.4 and 0.6 ms) show a 40–80% likelihood of being 'activated' by drug application.
source: Notably, the intermediate TP latency of 'activated' units is not the result of an equal distribution between high and low values. Units with intermediate TP latency (between 0.4 and 0.6 ms) are unique in showing a 40–80% likelihood of being 'activated' by drug application (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Release of 5-HT in vitro, induced by Fen application (200 µM), caused a suppression of SOs similar to what was observed in vivo.
source: Release of 5-HT in vitro, induced by Fen application (200 µM), caused a suppression of SOs similar to what we observed in vivo (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Application of low concentrations of 5-HT (5 µM) resulted in the suppression of SOs.
source: Likewise, application of low concentrations of 5-HT (5 µM) resulted in the suppression of SOs (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B,C.

claim: The suppression of SOs by 5-HT was highly consistent across different slices and was readily reversible.
source: This effect was highly consistent across different slices and was readily reversible (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Electrically evoked upstates were also suppressed by 5-HT.
source: Similarly to spontaneous upstates, electrically evoked upstates (Neske et al., 2015) were also suppressed by 5-HT (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Increasing the stimulation intensity did not rescue upstate generation during 5-HT application.
source: Increasing the stimulation intensity did not rescue upstate generation, indicating that a lack of excitation alone cannot explain the suppressive effect of 5-HT on SO.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from stimulation experiments.

claim: A lack of excitation alone cannot explain the suppressive effect of 5-HT on SO.
source: Increasing the stimulation intensity did not rescue upstate generation, indicating that a lack of excitation alone cannot explain the suppressive effect of 5-HT on SO.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental result that increasing stimulation did not rescue upstates.

claim: A substantial subset of EC excitatory neurons is known to express 5-HT1A receptor (5-HT1AR) and hyperpolarize upon 5-HT application via activation of G protein-coupled inwardly rectifying potassium (GIRK) channels.
source: A substantial subset of EC excitatory neurons is known to express 5-HT1A receptor (5-HT1AR) and hyperpolarize upon 5-HT application via activation of G protein-coupled inwardly rectifying potassium (GIRK) channels (Schmitz et al., 1998; Chalmers and Watson, 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Schmitz et al., 1998; Chalmers and Watson, 1991.

claim: The suppression of SOs by 5-HT was not influenced by blocking 5-HT1AR (WAY 100635, 100 nM).
source: The suppression of SOs by 5-HT, however, was not influenced by blocking 5-HT1AR (WAY 100635, 100 nM) (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A,E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A,E.

claim: Blocking 5-HT3R (tropisetron, 1 µM) did not have any impact on SOs suppression induced by 5-HT.
source: Blocking 5-HT3R (tropisetron, 1 µM), the receptor that characterizes one of the three main groups of interneurons, also did not have any impact on SOs suppression induced by 5-HT.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from pharmacological experiments.

claim: Application of the 5-HT3R agonist m-CPBG (50 µM) did not have any effect on SOs.
source: Similarly, application of the 5-HT3R agonist m-CPBG (50 µM) did not have any effect on SOs (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: Blocking 5-HT2AR with the selective antagonist ketanserin (1 µM) strongly reduced the suppression power of 5-HT on SOs from 95 ± 4% to 57 ± 10.1%.
source: In contrast, blocking 5-HT2AR with the selective antagonist ketanserin (1 µM) (Preller et al., 2018) strongly reduced the suppression power of 5-HT on SOs from 95 ± 4% to 57 ± 10.1% (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,E (note: this appears to be a typo in the manuscript, should be Figure 3—figure supplement 3).

claim: Selective activation of 5-HT2AR by α-methyl-5-HT (5 µM) mimicked the suppression of SOs observed after 5-HT wash-in.
source: Selective activation of 5-HT2AR by α-methyl-5-HT (5 µM) mimicked the suppression of SOs observed after 5-HT wash-in (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C,E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3C,E.

claim: 5-HT2AR activation causes an increase in intracellular calcium and consequent depolarization of the resting potential (RP).
source: 5-HT2AR activation is known to cause an increase in intracellular calcium and consequent depolarization of the resting potential (RP) (Nichols and Nichols, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Nichols and Nichols, 2008.

claim: After 5-HT application, a small group of neurons was depolarized (n = 6/48, 12.5%).
source: Accordingly, after 5-HT application, we found that a small group of neurons was depolarized (n = 6/48, 12.5%) (Figure 3—figure supplement 6B–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 6B–C.

claim: The cells excited by 5-HT belonged exclusively to the LTS group.
source: Strikingly, the cells excited by 5-HT belonged exclusively to the LTS group (Figure 3G, Figure 3—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G, Figure 3—figure supplement 6.

claim: A substantial proportion of LTS neurons express Sst.
source: A substantial proportion of LTS neurons express Sst (Tremblay et al., 2016; Gibson et al., 1999); therefore, we performed targeted patch-clamp recordings using a mouse line expressing tdTomato specifically in Sst-expressing interneurons (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Tremblay et al., 2016; Gibson et al., 1999.

claim: Sst interneurons depolarized upon 5-HT application (n = 19, ∆RP: 7.5 ± 1.23 mV).
source: Sst interneurons depolarized upon 5-HT application (n = 19, ∆RP: 7.5 ± 1.23 mV) (Figure 3I–L) and in some cases continued to spike while SOs were suppressed (n = 8/17, 47.05%, mean spiking rate = 3.03 ± 0.39 spikes/s).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3I–L.

claim: In some cases Sst interneurons continued to spike while SOs were suppressed (n = 8/17, 47.05%, mean spiking rate = 3.03 ± 0.39 spikes/s).
source: Sst interneurons depolarized upon 5-HT application (n = 19, ∆RP: 7.5 ± 1.23 mV) (Figure 3I–L) and in some cases continued to spike while SOs were suppressed (n = 8/17, 47.05%, mean spiking rate = 3.03 ± 0.39 spikes/s).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from recordings of Sst interneurons.

claim: The depolarization effect of 5-HT on Sst interneurons was blocked by ketanserin (n = 22).
source: This effect was blocked by ketanserin (n = 22) (Figure 3L).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3L.

claim: 11.8 ± 2.9% of the 5-HT2AR positive cells in EC colocalized with Sst (n = 7 mice).
source: We confirmed the presence of 5-HT2AR in Sst interneurons using immunohistochemistry in mice expressing EGFP under the 5-HT2AR promoter. In accordance with a previous study we found the majority of 5-HT2AR positive cells in the deep layers of EC, with a peak in L6 (Weber and Andrade, 2010). We observed that 11.8 ± 2.9% of the 5-HT2AR positive cells in EC colocalized with Sst (n = 7 mice) (Figure 3—figure supplement 9).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 9.

claim: The majority of 5-HT2AR positive cells in EC are found in the deep layers, with a peak in L6.
source: We confirmed the presence of 5-HT2AR in Sst interneurons using immunohistochemistry in mice expressing EGFP under the 5-HT2AR promoter. In accordance with a previous study we found the majority of 5-HT2AR positive cells in the deep layers of EC, with a peak in L6 (Weber and Andrade, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and a citation to Weber and Andrade, 2010.

claim: Light-stimulation of ChR2-expressing Sst interneurons in vitro suppressed SOs consistently.
source: Light-stimulation of ChR2- expressing Sst interneurons in vitro suppressed SOs consistently (Figure 4D–F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D–F.

claim: Light-stimulation of ChR2-expressing Sst interneurons diminished upstate-associated spiking.
source: Expectedly, upstate-associated spiking was also diminished (Figure 4C,E,F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C,E,F.

claim: At the end of the light stimulation of Sst interneurons, spontaneous upstates immediately reoccurred.
source: At the end of the light stimulation, spontaneous upstates immediately reoccurred (Figure 4G–H), in line with a critical role of Sst interneurons in the modulation of SOs (Fanselow et al., 2008; Funk et al., 2017; Niethard et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4G–H.

claim: Activation of PV interneurons can cause a similar suppression of SOs as Sst interneurons.
source: We acknowledge that activation of PV interneurons can cause a similar suppression (Zucca et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Zucca et al., 2017.

claim: Following application of 5-HT, a strong reduction of upstate incidence was observed, which was partially restored by subsequent application of CNO in Sst-hM4Di mice.
source: Following application of 5-HT we observed a strong reduction of upstate incidence, which was partially restored by subsequent application of CNO (Figure 5A–B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A–B.

claim: In experiments where CNO was applied before 5-HT in Sst-hM4Di mice, the significant reduction in upstate incidence typically seen after 5-HT wash-in was not observed.
source: Additionally, in further experiments in which CNO was applied before 5-HT, the significant reduction in upstate incidence typically seen after 5-HT wash-in was not observed (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: CNO did not show any significant effect in both wild-type littermates and hM4Di-PV mice.
source: CNO did not show any significant effect in both wild-type littermates and hM4Di-PV mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 2), indicating that the results observed are due to its specific effect on the activity of Sst interneurons.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The results observed with CNO are due to its specific effect on the activity of Sst interneurons.
source: CNO did not show any significant effect in both wild-type littermates and hM4Di-PV mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 2), indicating that the results observed are due to its specific effect on the activity of Sst interneurons.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the control experiments showing CNO has no effect in wild-type and PV-hM4Di mice.

claim: Activation of Sst interneurons either via 5-HT or directly by ChR2 suppresses SOs.
source: In summary, while activation of Sst interneurons either via 5-HT or directly by ChR2 suppresses SOs, the pharmacogenetic inactivation of Sst interneurons weakens the effect of 5-HT on SOs.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings from optogenetic and pharmacological experiments.

claim: The pharmacogenetic inactivation of Sst interneurons weakens the effect of 5-HT on SOs.
source: In summary, while activation of Sst interneurons either via 5-HT or directly by ChR2 suppresses SOs, the pharmacogenetic inactivation of Sst interneurons weakens the effect of 5-HT on SOs.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings from pharmacogenetic experiments.

claim: Sst interneurons have been previously proposed to provide the inhibition necessary for the termination of upstates, due to their strongly facilitating synapses.
source: Sst interneurons have been previously proposed to provide the inhibition necessary for the termination of upstates, due to their strongly facilitating synapses (Krishnamurthy et al., 2012; Melamed et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Krishnamurthy et al., 2012; Melamed et al., 2008.

claim: Increased inhibition can counteract temporal summation of inputs and reduce correlation due to tracking of shared inputs between inhibitory and excitatory populations.
source: Additionally, increased inhibition, as shown both in computational models and experimental data, can counteract temporal summation of inputs and reduce correlation due to tracking of shared inputs between inhibitory and excitatory populations (Sippy and Yuste, 2013; Renart et al., 2010; Stringer et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sippy and Yuste, 2013; Renart et al., 2010; Stringer et al., 2016.

claim: Sst interneurons are sufficient to cause desynchronization in V1.
source: Sst interneurons are specifically known to be sufficient to cause desynchronization in V1 (Chen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Chen et al., 2015.

claim: Sst interneurons are potently excited by ACh in various cortical areas, including mEC.
source: While it is well known that Sst interneurons are potently excited by ACh in various cortical areas (Chen et al., 2015; Obermayer et al., 2018; Fanselow et al., 2008), including mEC (Desikan et al., 2018) and NE in frontal cortex (Kawaguchi and Kubota, 1998), our work identifies them as a novel target of 5-HT regulation via 5-HT2AR.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2015; Obermayer et al., 2018; Fanselow et al., 2008; Desikan et al., 2018.

claim: Sst interneurons are excited by NE in frontal cortex.
source: While it is well known that Sst interneurons are potently excited by ACh in various cortical areas (Chen et al., 2015; Obermayer et al., 2018; Fanselow et al., 2008), including mEC (Desikan et al., 2018) and NE in frontal cortex (Kawaguchi and Kubota, 1998), our work identifies them as a novel target of 5-HT regulation via 5-HT2AR.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kawaguchi and Kubota, 1998.

claim: Inhibitory interneurons play a key role in mediating the effect of ACh and NE on cortical state transitions.
source: Recently, it has been proposed that inhibitory interneurons play a key role in mediating the effect of ACh and NE on cortical state transitions (Cardin, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Cardin, 2019.

claim: The excitation of Sst interneurons by 5-HT possibly contributes to the net inhibitory effect of 5-HT release observed in many cortical areas.
source: The excitation of Sst interneurons by 5-HT possibly contributes to the net inhibitory effect of 5-HT release observed in many cortical areas (Grandjean et al., 2019; Seillier et al., 2017; Azimi et al., 2020), and could explain why the inhibition strength is linearly correlated to 5-HT2AR expression (Grandjean et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the study's findings and supported by citations to Grandjean et al., 2019; Seillier et al., 2017; Azimi et al., 2020.

claim: The inhibition strength is linearly correlated to 5-HT2AR expression.
source: The excitation of Sst interneurons by 5-HT possibly contributes to the net inhibitory effect of 5-HT release observed in many cortical areas (Grandjean et al., 2019; Seillier et al., 2017; Azimi et al., 2020), and could explain why the inhibition strength is linearly correlated to 5-HT2AR expression (Grandjean et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Grandjean et al., 2019.

claim: Sst interneurons in the somatosensory cortex show increased cFos levels following 5-HT2AR activation.
source: Giving further support to this idea, Sst interneurons in the somatosensory cortex show increased cFos levels following 5-HT2AR activation (Martin and Nichols, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Martin and Nichols, 2016.

claim: Sst interneurons strongly influence dendritic computations and directly modulate perceptual thresholds.
source: A wealth of evidence suggests that active dendritic processing in cortical pyramidal neurons has a critical influence on sensory perception (Takahashi et al., 2016; Murayama et al., 2009; Smith et al., 2013; Ranganathan et al., 2018) and, in accordance with their unique anatomical properties, Sst interneurons strongly influence dendritic computations and directly modulate perceptual thresholds (Takahashi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Takahashi et al., 2016; Murayama et al., 2009; Smith et al., 2013; Ranganathan et al., 2018.

claim: Active dendritic processing in cortical pyramidal neurons has a critical influence on sensory perception.
source: A wealth of evidence suggests that active dendritic processing in cortical pyramidal neurons has a critical influence on sensory perception (Takahashi et al., 2016; Murayama et al., 2009; Smith et al., 2013; Ranganathan et al., 2018) and, in accordance with their unique anatomical properties, Sst interneurons strongly influence dendritic computations and directly modulate perceptual thresholds (Takahashi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Takahashi et al., 2016; Murayama et al., 2009; Smith et al., 2013; Ranganathan et al., 2018.

claim: Sst interneurons form synapses on the dendrites of their target cell, in contrast to PV interneurons.
source: Sst interneurons, in contrast to PV interneurons, form synapses on the dendrites of their target cell (Tremblay et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Tremblay et al., 2016.

claim: The novel link between 5-HT2AR and Sst interneurons might help elucidate the mechanisms underlying a host of psychiatric disorders.
source: We propose that the novel link between 5-HT2AR and Sst interneurons might help elucidate the mechanisms underlying a host of psychiatric disorders and contribute to our understanding of how serotonergic drugs exert their psychological effects.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal based on the study's findings.

claim: The novel link between 5-HT2AR and Sst interneurons might contribute to our understanding of how serotonergic drugs exert their psychological effects.
source: We propose that the novel link between 5-HT2AR and Sst interneurons might help elucidate the mechanisms underlying a host of psychiatric disorders and contribute to our understanding of how serotonergic drugs exert their psychological effects.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal based on the study's findings.

claim: Broadband reduction in oscillatory power, triggered by 5-HT2AR, seems to be linked to the subjective effect of serotonergic drugs.
source: Broadband reduction in oscillatory power, triggered by 5-HT2AR, seems to be linked to the subjective effect of serotonergic drugs (Carhart-Harris et al., 2016; Carhart-Harris and Friston, 2019) and has been consistently observed in humans and rodents following administration of MDMA (Frei et al., 2001; Lansbergen et al., 2011) or various other 5-HT2AR agonists (Kometer et al., 2015; Muthukumaraswamy et al., 2013; Carhart-Harris et al., 2016; Wood et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Carhart-Harris et al., 2016; Carhart-Harris and Friston, 2019; Frei et al., 2001; Lansbergen et al., 2011; Kometer et al., 2015; Muthukumaraswamy et al., 2013; Wood et al., 2012.

claim: Broadband reduction in oscillatory power has been consistently observed in humans and rodents following administration of MDMA.
source: Broadband reduction in oscillatory power, triggered by 5-HT2AR, seems to be linked to the subjective effect of serotonergic drugs (Carhart-Harris et al., 2016; Carhart-Harris and Friston, 2019) and has been consistently observed in humans and rodents following administration of MDMA (Frei et al., 2001; Lansbergen et al., 2011) or various other 5-HT2AR agonists (Kometer et al., 2015; Muthukumaraswamy et al., 2013; Carhart-Harris et al., 2016; Wood et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Frei et al., 2001; Lansbergen et al., 2011.

claim: Several routinely used antipsychotic drugs are potent 5-HT2AR antagonists.
source: The link between 5-HT2AR and perception is further supported by the fact that several routinely used antipsychotic drugs are potent 5-HT2AR antagonists (Marek et al., 2003; Meltzer, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Marek et al., 2003; Meltzer, 1999.

claim: Sst interneurons should be more active during states with higher 5-HT levels (wake>SWS>REM).
source: How does this notion relate to activation of Sst interneurons by 5-HT2AR? A limitation of our study is the absence of data in naturalistic conditions, with anesthesia potentially being a confounding factor (Adesnik et al., 2012). We can nonetheless speculate that Sst interneurons should be more active during states with higher 5-HT levels (wake>SWS>REM).
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the relationship between 5-HT levels and sleep-wake states.

claim: Sst interneurons in the dorsal cortical surface display their highest activity during waking states, lower activity during SWS and lowest activity during REM.
source: A previous study directly measuring the activity of various neuronal classes across different states seems to support this idea. Sst interneurons in the dorsal cortical surface display their highest activity during waking states, lower activity during SWS and lowest activity during REM (Niethard et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Niethard et al., 2016.

claim: Dopamine can suppress SOs in vitro.
source: For example, it is known that dopamine can suppress SOs in vitro (Mayne et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Mayne et al., 2013.

claim: Fenfluramine has been reported to selectively increase 5-HT concentration in the brain.
source: Fen, however, has been reported to selectively increase 5-HT concentration in the brain (Rothman and Baumann, 2002) and has been used previously to specifically disentangle the effect of MDMA on different neuromodulatory systems (Heifets et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Rothman and Baumann, 2002; Heifets et al., 2019.

claim: 5-HT is associated with the etiology of various psychiatric disorders, as are Sst interneurons.
source: Besides its involvement in various physiological brain processes, 5-HT is also associated with the etiology of various psychiatric disorders, as are Sst interneurons (Pantazopoulos et al., 2017; Lin and Sibille, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Pantazopoulos et al., 2017; Lin and Sibille, 2015.

claim: 5-HT2AR activation has been reported to be essential for the psychological effects induced by various psychedelics.
source: Furthermore, 5-HT is linked to the psychological effect of many psychotropic drugs; specifically, 5-HT2AR activation has been reported to be essential for the psychological effects induced by various psychedelics (Nichols, 2016), and in the case of MDMA, has been linked to perceptual and emotional alterations (Liechti et al., 2000; Kuypers et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Nichols, 2016.

claim: In the case of MDMA, 5-HT2AR activation has been linked to perceptual and emotional alterations.
source: Furthermore, 5-HT is linked to the psychological effect of many psychotropic drugs; specifically, 5-HT2AR activation has been reported to be essential for the psychological effects induced by various psychedelics (Nichols, 2016), and in the case of MDMA, has been linked to perceptual and emotional alterations (Liechti et al., 2000; Kuypers et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Liechti et al., 2000; Kuypers et al., 2018.
